strengths: Well-motivated and clearly presented idea: using language descriptions as an additional conditioning signal in a Stable Diffusion-based depth estimator (Marigold-style). The pipeline figure and method description are easy to follow.

The paper demonstrates a genuinely interesting capability: controllable depth estimation (Fig. 6), where adding a sentence about a specific object improves the predicted depth for that region. This user-in-the-loop controllability is a distinctive feature that most prior depth estimators lack.

The evaluation is reasonably thorough: zero-shot evaluation on four real-world benchmarks (NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet), sub-analyses for small-area masks using MaskDINO (Table 2), denoising-step ablations (Table 4 / Fig. 8), prompt/description ablations (Table 3), and template-prompt fallback experiments (Table 5). The supplementary adds useful detail.

A modest but real efficiency benefit is shown: comparable accuracy to Marigold at 20K iterations vs Marigold's 30K, with a faster convergence curve (Fig. 7) and good performance at very low denoising steps (Table 4).
The authors acknowledge limitations honestly (dependence on description quality, shown in the misleading-text failure case in Fig. 9).
weaknesses: The quantitative gains over Marigold are marginal and likely within run-to-run noise. In Table 1, on NYUv2 PriorDiffusion (30K) gives δ1=96.0/AbsRel=5.9 vs Marigold (74K) 95.7/6.1; on ScanNet 94.9/6.7 vs Marigold 94.5/6.9; ETH3D 95.8/6.5 vs 95.1/7.1. On KITTI the gain over the re-implemented Marigold* is somewhat larger (90.6 vs 86.2 at 20K) but still comparable to Marigold's original 74K number (90.4). Claims of 'state-of-the-art' performance are overstated; the method is essentially on par, not better.

The 'language prior' is largely circular. Descriptions are generated by LLaVA from the same input image, so the text is a re-encoding of visual content already present. This makes it unclear whether the method adds information beyond the image or merely acts as an auxiliary attention/feature cue. The paper repeatedly frames this as a 'human-provided' prior, but no actual human descriptions are used; the ablation in Table 3 varies LLaVA prompts, not human vs. machine text.

The comparison to prior work that uses language for depth estimation (DepthCLIP, WorDepth, RSA, which are cited in Related Work) is entirely absent. For a paper whose central claim is that language priors improve depth estimation, the lack of direct comparison to existing language-based depth methods is a material omission.

The contribution is incremental over Marigold: the backbone, training data, normalization, evaluation protocol, and diffusion formulation are essentially inherited, and the only methodological change is conditioning on real text rather than empty/null text. This limits the technical novelty.

The 'faster convergence' benefit is modest (20K vs 30K iterations, both reported at ~4 days on a single RTX 3090) and does not clearly translate into a meaningful inference-time or compute advantage, especially since LLaVA must be run to produce descriptions at test time—an extra cost that is not quantified.

The reported improvements on small areas (Table 2) are also small (e.g., 95.9 vs 95.7 standard, 93.1 vs 92.2 for 10% area) and could fall within variance; no error bars or multiple-seed results are reported, so the significance of the deltas is unestablished.

The controllability demonstration (Fig. 6, Figs. 10–11) is qualitative and cherry-picked; while illustrative, it is not quantitatively validated (e.g., no measurement that the specified region's depth actually improves by a measurable margin), so the strength of this claim is hard to assess.
